<h1 align="center">CASTAWAY</h1>

<p align="center">
  <b>A ten-hour lo-fi island video in which almost nothing happens, exactly on the beat.</b><br>
  <sub>Working title. In development. An unofficial remake inspired by <i>Johnny Castaway</i>, the 1992 desert-island screensaver.</sub>
</p>

<p align="center">
  <a href="tools/serve.py"><b>run it</b></a> &nbsp;·&nbsp;
  <a href="activities.toml">the schedule</a> &nbsp;·&nbsp;
  <a href="tools/make_audio.py">the sound</a> &nbsp;·&nbsp;
  <a href="MUSING.md">the notes</a>
</p>

A stationary-frame video for YouTube, in the spirit of the ten-hour lofi streams: a young woman alone on a tiny island with one tall palm, a raft and a lot of time. She idles, nodding to the music in her cream headphones, and every so often something happens. A message in a bottle washes straight back. A shark in headphones nods along. A coconut falls on a hermit crab, and the crab walks off wearing it. 16:9, 1080p, sunny hand-painted coastal anime, and always daytime.

Up there is the same video as a 1990s music visualiser would see it: one line, and everything it just did, on fire. No visualiser has ever had less to react to, and this one has made the most of it. It is also the only thing so far that has reacted to the soundtrack at all, although, to be fair, it is reading the sheet music.

More than 90 activities live in [activities.toml](activities.toml), on four timers: something regular every 2 to 5 minutes, occasional every 12 to 25, rare every 30 to 60, and super rare every 3 to 6 hours. Every one of them waits for the next bar of the music (every 3 seconds), so even the nothing lands on the beat. Every sound is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, no loops, no recordings, so no third-party licence applies.

```sh
python tools/serve.py
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```

Live preview in the page, then export a YouTube-ready MP4: the browser encodes frame-exact H.264 with WebCodecs, and the server mixes in the sound and joins the two. Plain ES modules, no build step, no npm. [`python tools/schedule.py`](tools/schedule.py) validates the schedule and simulates a ten-hour run; [`python tools/render_demo.py --dev`](tools/render_demo.py) renders a dev reel of every activity. Nothing is published yet, so for now the only way to watch her do nothing for ten hours is to run it yourself.

<details>
<summary><b>NOW PLAYING</b>: the banner's 24 seconds, bar by bar</summary>

```text
 BAR  TIME   CHORD  FLOW        PALETTE  ON THE LINE
 ───  ─────  ─────  ──────────  ───────  ──────────────────────────────────
 13   00:00  Gm9    SWELL       CORAL    nothing happening, on schedule
 14   00:03  C13    WHIRLPOOL   CORAL    still nothing (lovely)
 15   00:06  Fmaj9  HEAT HAZE   KUMARA   a fin in headphones cruises in
 16   00:09  Dm9    EDDY        KUMARA   it nods on the beat, then dives
 17   00:12  Gm9    TRADE WIND  LAGOON   a bottle goes out, message inside
 18   00:15  C13    UNDERTOW    LAGOON   it comes straight back; no reply
 19   00:18  Fmaj9  HEAT HAZE   MANGO    one bar of signal, top of the palm
 20   00:21  Dm9    SWELL       MANGO    nothing happening again
```

These are bars 13 to 20 of the real theme, a seamless 60-second loop at 80 BPM in F major: 20 bars of exactly 3 seconds, a ii-V-I-vi (Gm9, C13, Fmaj9, Dm9, one chord a bar) on electric piano, with a kalimba lead, soft drums and vinyl crackle. The banner's waveform is computed from the score in [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): every kalimba note, the kick on 1 and on the and-of-3, the snare on 2 and 4, and the breakdown at bar 17, where the drums drop to kick and rim. High notes shake the narrow wiggles, the kick shakes the wide ones, and every hit ripples outward from the island. It is drawn from the notes, not from the audio file, because nobody has listened to the audio file yet. That includes the visualiser.

The real video spaces its gags minutes and hours apart. The banner books a shark and a bottle into the same 24 seconds, which by island standards is a very busy day.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>SLOWBURN.CFG</b>: what the visualiser is waiting for</summary>

```ini
; SLOWBURN.CFG  ·  input settings for a very quiet ten hours
; (counts: median of 200 simulated runs, as activities.toml says)

[input]
picture      = one island, one palm, one raft, one young woman
sound        = synthesized from code, more than 150 files so far
theme        = 60 s loop, 80 BPM, F major, 20 bars of 3 s
level        = -14 LUFS, true peak at or below -1 dBTP
heard_by     = nobody yet

[events]                            ; more than 90 activities in all
regular      = every 2 to 5 min     ; about 155 a run
occasional   = every 12 to 25 min   ; about 30 a run
rare         = every 30 to 60 min   ; about 13 a run
super_rare   = every 3 to 6 h       ; about 2 a run, never more than 3
chained      = follow-ups only      ; e.g. the tide takes the sandcastle
quantize     = 1 bar                ; nothing starts off the beat

[mood]
busy         = about a third        ; the rest is idling, on purpose
lanes        = on                   ; visitors may turn up mid-routine
run          = 10:00:00             ; seed 1992
time_of_day  = day                  ; always; it is a project rule
```

Lanes are why the classic joke works: she has one lane, and the cat, the turtle, the sea and sky, and the shore each have their own, so a visitor can sail past exactly while she is busy with a coconut. The schedule even waits for her to get busy first.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>SETUP</b>: four palettes, eight flows</summary>
<br>
<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/96-feedback-fire_opus_5.5-setup.svg" width="100%" alt="The setup screen. Left, four palettes, each nine steps from black to white, two bars each: CORAL (bars 13-14), KUMARA (15-16), LAGOON (17-18) and MANGO (19-20). Right, eight small black tiles, one per bar, each with the line across it and a field of arrows showing where half a second of that flow drags each part of the screen: SWELL pushes everything outward from a point above the line, WHIRLPOOL turns it clockwise, HEAT HAZE lifts it, EDDY turns it back the other way, TRADE WIND blows it left, UNDERTOW pulls it right and down, then HEAT HAZE and SWELL again.">
</p>

The real programs of 1993 to 1998 did two things, over and over: draw the sound wave into the picture, then replace the picture with a slightly warped, slightly darker copy of itself. Brightness went through a palette, so anything fading looked like it was cooling: white, then yellow, then red, then gone. Every so often, on a beat, the warp switched to a different map and the flames changed direction.

The four palettes are named after things on, or near, the island. The kumara is the one she plants, which grows over the course of the video. The eight flows are named after what the sea and the air are doing, if you squint. Nothing on the island is actually on fire. It is a palette.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>HOW THE FIRE IS FAKED</b>: an SVG has no frame buffer</summary>

A real feedback visualiser keeps last frame's picture and warps it. An SVG cannot remember anything from one frame to the next, so this is an imitation of feedback, not feedback, and it is honest about it.

**The echo stack.** The line is drawn 21 times. Copy *k* is the line as it was *k* × 0.08 seconds ago (its animations simply run late), moved by exactly the warp that the real thing would have applied to it since: the generator composes the flow maps for that stretch of time, numerically, and bakes the result into three animated transforms per copy. When the flow switches on a bar line, the kink travels outward through the copies, the way it does on the real screen. Older copies are dimmer and wider.

**The fire.** All the copies go through one SVG filter: fractal noise pushes them around (the push breathes in and out every 6 seconds), a blur softens them, a second, finer noise adds the speckle (the real thing carried each pixel's rounding error into the next one), and lookup tables map brightness to colour. The tables are animated, so the palette drifts. Last, one point is sampled from every 4 × 4 block and spread over the block, so the fire is a 320 × 100 picture, as chunky as those screens were.

**The line.** The waveform is a row of half-wave lobes between fixed zero crossings, each one stretched up or down by an envelope computed from the score, so the line never breaks. The island, the palm, the fin and the bottle are drawn into the same line and burn like everything else, just at a lower heat, or the white line would vanish into its own white-hot wake. They also get a faint dark edge, for the same reason.

**The lettering** is a 5 × 7 pixel font drawn for this header, one path per glyph, never system text. **Reduced motion** shows a still: the line just after the downbeat of bar 13, its echoes where the swell has put them, palette CORAL. **Weight**: the filter repaints the whole banner every frame, so a phone or an old laptop may run it at a modest frame rate. It still looks like fire, just a calmer one.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>GREETINGS FROM THE TOP OF THE PALM</b></summary>
<br>

To the island regulars, who are the only reason the line ever moves: the shark, for wearing headphones and keeping time; the bottle, for coming straight back, and the other bottle, for one day bringing a reply; the sea turtle, who visits; the stray cat (grey tabby, white chest), who arrives on a crate, naps up the palm, floats off one day and comes back another; the delivery drone, whose parcel is another pair of headphones; the hermit crab, for wearing a coconut with dignity; the bro on the electric hydrofoil, shaka received; the tour boat of selfie-takers; the kumara, growing as fast as it can; and the one bar of signal, which is at the top of the palm and nowhere else.

To the feedback visualisers of 1993 to 1998, Cthugha on DOS and the Geiss plug-in for Winamp (whose author wrote down exactly how it worked): credited here as the inspiration for the look. Nothing of theirs is copied. The palettes, flows, font, island and code are all made from scratch, and SLOWBURN is made up.

</details>
